newsitem.title: USA: Sixteen U.S. children die of gunfire every day.
newsitem.headline: Sixteen U.S. children die of gunfire every day.

text.p: By this time tomorrow, 16 more American children will be dead of gunfire. And in the time it takes to read this paragraph and the next, another American child will have been reported neglected or abused.
These were among the grim statistics in a new report released on Wednesday by the Washington-based Children's Defence Fund about the rising tide of violence facing the youngest U.S. citizens.
It said the United States had the dubious distinction of leading the industrialised world in child firearm deaths. It not only leads the others, but is leaps and bounds ahead.

"In 1993, the year for which the most recent complete data are available, 5,721 children under 20 died from gunfire -- one child every hour and a half, or the equivalent of a classroomful of children every two days," the report said.
Fund researchers estimates there are about 78 million people in America under 20.
"U.S. children under 15 die from gunfire at a rate 12 times higher than the combined rates of 25 other industrialised countries," the document said.

The report, called "The State of America's Children," is released every year by the Fund, a non-profit organisation that seeks to educate Americans about childrens' problems and encourage policies and actions to help prevent and solve them.

This year's document is full of depressing news about American kids. As a group they are the poorest U.S. citizens: one in five lives below the official poverty line. A record number of them, nearly ten million, lack health insurance. Every day six of them commit suicide.
Every ten seconds a child is reported abused or neglected, and every day three children die from abuse or neglect.

The number of children reported abused or neglected in 1995 marked an almost 25 percent increase over 1990 figures, and the authors of the report worry that a new welfare reform law will put more children at risk as it adds to families' financial stress.
But unlike other industrialised countries, the rise in child deaths in the United States appears driven by the easy availability of guns, in both deliberate and accidental shootings, the report said.
It said the U.S. child gun deaths recorded in 1993 were nearly twice the number of a decade earlier and blamed "a tidal wave of guns into communities" for the dramatic increase.
"Gun crime is virtually the only type of youth crime that has risen over the past decade," the report said.

"Because juveniles have increasingly easy access to guns, what formerly would have been a fist fight or knife fight or a serious act of delinquency now too often involves a gun and is far more likely to result in death or a homicide arrest."

It urged more gun control -- in particular banning handguns known as "Saturday night specials" which have no sporting purpose -- and more crime prevention programmes that fund schools and community groups to operate after-school and summer programmes.
